newsitem.title: USA: Stocks are expected to remain under pressure this week.
newsitem.headline: Stocks are expected to remain under pressure this week.

text.p: Stocks are expected to remain under pressure this week, with investors facing a second round of congressional testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and a key report on the economy.
"It's going to be choppy," Charles Pradillo, a market analyst at Cowen and Co., said of the market's expected action this week.
Greenspan sent a chill down Wall Street last Wednesday by saying in the first half of his semi-annual report to Congress that stocks' recent rapid rise has "raised questions of sustainability."
The Dow industrials lost lost 47 points Friday to close at 6,878, down 54 points for the week.
The Dow shot up 10 percent -- and cracked the 7,000 level -- in the weeks after Greenspan first warned in early December of investors' "irrational exuberance."
But this time, especially given the sharp runup in stocks, investors are showing a greater reluctance to push stock prices higher, analysts said.
"You can only ignore him for so long," Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd, said.
Greenspan will appear Wednesday before the House Banking sub-committee in the second half of his so-called Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
Market players said they will be watching for any elaboration by the Fed chairman on his stock market comments as well as looking for any hints of the Fed raising short-term interest rates soon.
On Friday the government reports on February employment.
Any sign of further tightness in the labour market will stir up fears in the bond and stock markets over the possibility of an imminent Fed rate hike, which would be a major blow to the bull market.
"The jobs number is going to be very closely watched," Alice Hook, first vice president at McDonald & Co., said.
Technology stocks could come under further selling pressure this week as investors review the lofty levels the group reached during the recent rally, analysts said.
"There appears to be a revaluation in technology downwards over the near-term," Bleier said.
